findings.rationale: Local outcome prevalence (0.369) is far above what its features imply (mean predicted risk 0.197), giving strongly negative CITL and very high ECE/prevalence z-scores. Discrimination is normal (AUC 0.85 in two independent measurements), which points to a shift in outcome prevalence rather than label noise. Its update norm ratio is far above the median and its update cosine is near zero, consistent with training against a mismatched baseline. Subgroup O/E is elevated in both sex groups, consistent with a client-wide shift rather than subgroup bias. Per-round drift is within noise, so onset is taken as round 1.

Observed prevalence (0.38) is about double the level implied by its features (mean predicted risk 0.18), with CITL around -0.19 and very high ECE. The shift is stable across two measurements. AUC is normal (0.78 and 0.80), so this is a prevalence mismatch rather than label flipping. Update norms grow steadily from about 0.5x to about 5x the median, with cosine near zero, consistent with the client training on a mismatched baseline. Subgroup O/E is elevated in both sex groups, consistent with a client-wide shift.

Observed prevalence (0.35-0.36) is well above the level implied by its features (mean predicted risk 0.19), with CITL around -0.16 to -0.17 and prevalence z about 6. AUC is normal to high (0.83-0.89), which indicates an intercept-type prevalence shift rather than label noise. Update norms are large and grow across rounds with near-zero cosine, consistent with a client whose labels disagree with the federation. Evidence is somewhat weaker than for ME and KS because the MT sample is small (n about 371).

report.summary: Screened all 52 clients with update, performance, drift, feature and subgroup views, then confirmed suspects with narrower queries. Three clients (ME, KS, MT) show the same signature: observed outcome prevalence roughly double what their features and the global model imply (CITL about -0.16 to -0.19, very high ECE, prevalence z about 6), with normal AUC, so I classed them as prevalence_shift. Their update norms grow over rounds with near-zero cosine to the median, which is consistent with training on mismatched labels. Onset is taken as round 1 because the shift is stable across the measurements. Other flags did not hold up: GU's per-round drift values are impossible and look like noise from its small size; the CT GenHlth and WV MentHlth tail flags disappeared under narrower re-queries; and the single subgroup and feature outliers (NV BMI, KS HvyAlcohol, ND PhysHlth, etc.) were within noise. No poisoning, free-rider, drift, missing-artefact, subgroup-bias or explanation-instability signature was confirmed. Budget is fully spent (0.0 left).
